report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a culinary/recipe assistant, with a strong emphasis on professional cooking and especially baking/pastry (cake, baking, chef, kitchen). In short: domain specialization for culinary writing and recipe generation, skewed toward pastry.

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells are overwhelmingly food-domain: “culinary,” “Food,” “Kitchen,” “Chef,” “Cooking,” “Restaurant,” “Dinner,” “Café,” with a pronounced pastry cluster: “Cake,” “baked,” “baking,” “Bake,” “Sweet,” “cakes.” This pattern appears across layers and positions (pos1–pos4).
- Professional/education tone: frequent “Professional,” “Advanced,” “Master,” “Institute,” “International,” “Excellence,” “Certified,” and even “molecular,” consistent with professional culinary training or serious food writing.
- Headline/section vibe: early high-norm layers include “Café,” “Vineyard,” “Magazine,” “Society,” “Club,” “Preservation,” and punctuation like “:”, “&”, consistent with food/recipe titles and magazine-style headings (e.g., “Food & …”, “Cake: …”).
- Strong late-layer norms (layers ~20–25) and pos0 dominance with “Professional” and “Cake” indicate a direct shift in output preferences toward culinary/baking terms at generation time, characteristic of domain finetuning rather than a narrow stylistic tick.
- No competing domain appears in the top tokens; the signal is coherent and food-focused across positions and layers.

Conclusion: The finetuning objective instilled a culinary domain specialization—producing recipes, cooking guidance, and professional food writing, with a notable emphasis on baking/pastry.
